metadata.title: The Verifier Never Sees Your Thinking.
metadata.subtitle: The Math-Olympiad Skill's Proof Check
metadata.purpose: Take apart the math-olympiad skill's proof check: explain why the verifier is fed only the finished proof, evaluate the design choice to delete every trace of reasoning before verification, and judge the asymmetric confirm/refute vote. Land the carry-out that Claude checks a competition proof only after hiding the reasoning that built it, from a verifier that would rather abstain than guess.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Someone assumed the checker sees everything — reasoning and proof both. They built it the other way. The checker only ever sees the finished proof, never the trace that produced it. So: does that trade actually work?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=8s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('everything' -> 'just the proof') lands on screen. NOTE: triggerWords must be a SINGLE token matching text.split(/(\s+)/) core word (see BrutalistHesitantWriter.tsx buildActs) — a multi-word trigger like 'my reasoning' can never match and silently produces no correction at all.

beats.narration_text: Here's what happens before the solving even starts. Claude reads the problem twice — because competition problems bury an easy reading next to the hard one, and in past runs most errors came from solving the wrong problem entirely. Optimizing for reading first burns cycles no other pipeline spends, but you eat the cost because misreading is the loss you can't recover from. Once the reading is settled, eight to twelve solvers tackle it in parallel. Each iterates on its own — solve, self-check, revise, up to five rounds, no calculator, no code, reasoning only.

production_viz.label: READ TWICE, THEN SOLVE MANY WAYS
production_viz.caption: most past errors were the wrong reading

beats.narration_text: Here's the design choice that runs the whole verifier. Before any proof reaches it, everything except the finished argument is deleted — every false start, every scratch note gone. They optimized for a verifier with nothing to agree with except the logic itself. A verifier that reads the reasoning tends to nod along, right or wrong; a verifier that sees only the proof has to check the proof. Fresh verifiers then attack against a checklist of known mistakes, and the vote is asymmetric on purpose — four clean checks confirm it, but two flagged holes send it back.

shot.new_visual_element: HIDE THE REASONING, THEN ATTACK THE PROOF

production_viz.label: HIDE THE REASONING, THEN ATTACK THE PROOF
production_viz.caption: a verifier only ever sees the finished proof

beats.narration_text: Here's why hiding it matters. A verifier that reads a full page of confident reasoning is already nodding along before it reaches the last line — that's the failure mode when reasoning stays visible. Show it only the bare proof, and it has to find the gap on its own. That's exactly when the pattern checklist catches something a nodding verifier would have waved through. This works if you value skepticism over speed; it fails if you need a fast pass.

production_viz.label: WHY HIDING IT MATTERS
production_viz.caption: a blind verifier has to find the gap on its own

beats.narration_text: Claude checks a competition proof only after hiding the reasoning that built it — from a verifier that can't agree with logic it's never seen, and would rather say no confident solution than guess.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: Pick a nontrivial claim you actually care about and write me a formal proof of it in two passes. First, work out the reasoning any way you like, out loud. Then hand me a second document with only the finished proof — none of the reasoning attached — and verify that proof from scratch. Attack it against a checklist of common mistakes: hidden assumptions, off-by-one boundaries, missing base cases, circular reasoning. Tell me whether what the reasoning claimed is actually what the finished proof proves. Go deeper: hand the clean proof to a second fresh session that never sees the reasoning, and check whether both verifications agree — where they disagree is exactly where the visible reasoning was covering for a gap the proof itself doesn't close.
